curation.lead:
Jeffrey A. Schantz is a New York-based attorney who served as one of Jeffrey Epstein's most senior fiduciaries from at least 1996 until approximately 2003. Under Epstein's original 2001 estate plan, Schantz held extraordinary powers: co-Trustee of both the Jeffrey E. Epstein 2001 Trust One and Trust Two, co-Executor of Epstein's will alongside Paul Hoffman, and authority to designate and remove successor Executors and Trustees (Finding #1990). Trust One designated a $10 million bequest to Schantz upon Epstein's death — equal to the bequest to Epstein's brother Mark Lawrence Epstein — a figure that reflects the depth of Epstein's reliance on him (Finding #1987). Simultaneously, Schantz served as Vice President, Secretary, and Treasurer of multiple Epstein USVI corporations based at 6100 Red Hook Quarter, Suite B-3, American Yacht Harbor, St. Thomas (Finding #1992), and managed day-to-day operations at Epstein's NYSG LLC offices at 457 Madison Avenue, New York (Findings #1999, #2000).

Schantz's departure from Epstein's orbit occurred in 2003 through a rapid, systematic dismantling of all his fiduciary roles. The First Codicil to Epstein's will (June 27, 2003) replaced Schantz and Hoffman as executors with Henry Jarecki and Bruce Cayne. A Trust One amendment removed Schantz as co-Trustee and replaced him with Ghislaine Maxwell and Ira Zicherman — notably requiring two people to fill the role Schantz had held alone (Finding #2005). The Second Amendment to Trust One (December 2004) formally deleted the $10 million bequest: "I hereby delete Article FIRST, paragraph II, subparagraph c, which provides a bequest to JEFFREY A. SCHANTZ" (Finding #2003). A 2016 email between Mark Epstein and Jeffrey Epstein confirmed the timeline: "Does Jeff Schantz still work for you?" — "Left 13 years ago" (Finding #1995).

The circumstances of Schantz's departure remain investigatively significant. In October 2003, the same period as his exit, NYSG LLC transferred $500,000 to Schantz at his Hewlett, NY address, alongside a $200,000 transfer to Darren Indyke, both funded by a $1 million Epstein deposit the prior day (Finding #1994). Schantz had also provided sworn declarations in FTC v. Citibank (D.V.I. Civ. No. 2002-108), a case concerning a $10 million AIG-managed investment made via Citibank loan (Finding #2013). After leaving Epstein, Schantz left virtually no trace in federal court records as a named party — an unusual profile for an attorney described by the New York Post in 2003 as "Epstein's lawyer" (Finding #2010). His post-Epstein career includes a 2006 lobbying registration for JGW International Ltd on behalf of Protonex Technology Corporation, focused on defense and homeland security matters (Finding #2009).

sections.title: Key Relationships
sections.content:
Schantz's position in the Epstein network was defined by his role as the primary fiduciary counterpart to Jeffrey Epstein himself. From November 8, 2001, when the estate plan was formalized, Schantz served as co-Trustee of both Trust One and Trust Two and co-Executor of Epstein's will. His backup in the trustee hierarchy was Darren Indyke, confirming that Schantz outranked Indyke in the original structure (Finding #1990). The two men worked in proximity at NYSG LLC's 457 Madison Avenue offices, and both received large transfers from the entity in October 2003 — $500,000 to Schantz and $200,000 to Indyke (Finding #1994). After Schantz's departure, Indyke would go on to become Epstein's primary attorney for the next sixteen years.

Ghislaine Maxwell and Ira Zicherman were named as Schantz's direct successors as co-Trustees of Trust One (Finding #2005). The fact that Epstein needed two replacements where one had sufficed underscores the breadth of roles Schantz had occupied. Maxwell's notarization was handled by Harry Beller in New York, while Zicherman's was handled by Anna Vero, and Paul Hoffman — Schantz's co-officer in multiple USVI entities — notarized the removal document from the Virgin Islands. Hoffman and Schantz together had served as the founding trustees of the J. Epstein Virgin Islands Foundation alongside Epstein (Finding #2002), and as officers of at least three to four USVI corporations (Finding #1992).

In the 2012 restructuring of both trusts, Andrew Farkas and Jes Staley were named alongside Indyke to fill the trustee positions Schantz had once held. Farkas executed the amended agreements; Staley notably did not (Finding #2014). Kelly Bovino, the sole beneficiary of Trust Two upon Epstein's death, was a beneficiary of the trust structure that Schantz had co-administered. Joseph Pagano was named alongside Schantz as a potential director of a successor charitable organization under Trust One (Finding #1987), suggesting Pagano occupied a similar advisory tier.

sections.title: The Fiduciary Architecture
sections.content:
The concentration of fiduciary authority in Schantz was remarkable even by the standards of high-net-worth estate planning. Under Epstein's 2001 will and trust instruments, Schantz simultaneously held the roles of co-Trustee of Trust One, co-Trustee of Trust Two, co-Executor of the will, and was empowered to designate and remove successor Executors and Trustees (Finding #1990). This created a structure where, alongside Epstein, Schantz had effective control over the disposition of assets upon Epstein's death, the management of trust assets during Epstein's lifetime, and the governance succession of the entire estate apparatus.

Trust One contained the bulk of Epstein's known bequests: $10 million to Schantz, $10 million to Mark Lawrence Epstein, and provisions for a successor charitable organization. Trust Two, whose sole death beneficiary was Kelly Bovino at 100 percent, appears to have served as a separate vehicle — and the Second Amendment's redirection of $20 million from Trust One to Trust Two suggests the trusts functioned as a coordinated system rather than independent instruments (Finding #2014). Schantz's co-trusteeship of both trusts simultaneously gave him visibility into the full architecture.

The USVI corporate layer added further depth. Schantz held the triple role of Vice President, Secretary, and Treasurer across multiple Epstein entities incorporated in the U.S. Virgin Islands, with Paul Hoffman and Epstein as co-trustees on the boards (Finding #1992). This jurisdictional positioning — New York operations paired with USVI incorporation — is consistent with the tax and regulatory arbitrage strategies that characterized Epstein's broader financial structure. The 6100 Red Hook Quarter address at American Yacht Harbor, St. Thomas, served as the registered office for these entities.

sections.title: Financial Flows and Compensation
sections.content:
The most direct evidence of financial flows to Schantz comes from the NYSG LLC JPMorgan Private Bank statement for October 2003 (EFTA01514000). On October 16, Epstein funded NYSG LLC with a $1,000,000 transfer. The following day, October 17, NYSG executed a $500,000 book transfer to "Jeffrey A. Schantz, Hewlett NY 11557" and a $200,000 transfer to Darren Indyke (Finding #1994). The timing — immediately following Schantz's removal from the will in June 2003 and coinciding with his departure — raises the question of whether the $500,000 represented a separation payment, deferred compensation, or settlement of some other obligation.

The original $10 million bequest in Trust One (Finding #1987) provides a baseline for assessing how Epstein valued Schantz's role. This amount equaled the bequest to Epstein's own brother, placing Schantz at the level of family in the estate hierarchy. The December 2004 Second Amendment that deleted this bequest (Finding #2003) and simultaneously redirected $20 million to Trust Two suggests that Epstein restructured the financial architecture of his estate following Schantz's departure, not merely removing a name but reallocating the underlying assets.

FEC records show Schantz made a $2,000 donation to the Kerry Committee in 2002, listing NYSG LLC as his employer and Hewlett, NY as his residence. More recent donations from 2023 to 2025 show a bipartisan pattern including contributions to Nikki Haley ($1,597.50), Trump/NRSC ($427), and other committees (Finding #2006). The FTC v. Citibank litigation revealed that Schantz was involved in managing a $10 million investment originated August 2, 1999 via a Citibank loan, with the express condition that funds be used exclusively for an AIG-managed venture. This investment was amended on June 15, 2000, extending to August 2, 2001 (Finding #2013).

sections.title: Legal Proceedings and Regulatory Footprint
sections.content:
Schantz's most substantive appearance in litigation records is his sworn declaration in FTC v. Citibank (D.V.I. Civ. No. 2002-108), a case arising from the Financial Trust Company's $10 million investment via Citibank in an AIG-managed fund. The court opinion (EFTA01386058) details Schantz's role as FTC advisor and counsel: he contacted Citibank employee Davison seeking help replacing AIG as fund manager, participated in information-gathering from Citibank, Salomon Smith Barney (SSB), and Chase Manhattan about AIG fund investor identities, and was present for a telephone conference in August 2001 where SSB disclosed an investment banking conflict with AIG (Finding #2013). The parallel New York action, Citibank NA v. Epstein (SDNY 1:02-cv-05332, Judge Sidney H. Stein), was filed July 11, 2002, and terminated July 2003. Gerald B. Lefcourt entered an appearance in September 2003 representing both Epstein and Financial Trust Company — the same period Schantz departed (Finding #2011).

A comprehensive federal court search reveals zero cases with Jeffrey A. Schantz as a named party (Finding #2010). For an attorney identified in the press as "Epstein's lawyer" (New York Post, February 4, 2003, EFTA02729242), this absence is notable. It suggests Schantz operated behind the scenes — filing declarations, managing entities, and advising — rather than appearing as counsel of record or as a litigant. The Gerber v. Financial Trust Company case (SDNY 1:18-cv-07580, August 2018), while filed fifteen years after Schantz's departure, targeted the same entity where Schantz had served as advisor. That case was dismissed with prejudice within six weeks (Finding #2012).

Federal regulatory searches yield similarly sparse results. FARA records show zero registrations or foreign principal associations. LDA lobbying records reveal one registration: a "Jeff Schantz" (ID 29441) registered as a federal lobbyist for JGW International Ltd in 2006, lobbying on behalf of Protonex Technology Corporation on defense and homeland security matters (Finding #2009). Whether this is the same Jeffrey A. Schantz has not been conclusively confirmed, but the name, timing (post-Epstein departure), and defense-sector focus suggest a plausible post-Epstein career trajectory (Finding #2017).

sections.title: The 2003 Departure
sections.content:
The severing of Schantz from Epstein's legal and financial structures occurred with striking speed and thoroughness in 2003. The First Codicil to Epstein's will, dated June 27, 2003, replaced Schantz and Paul Hoffman as executors with Henry Jarecki and Bruce Cayne. A Trust One amendment removed Schantz as co-Trustee and installed Ghislaine Maxwell and Ira Zicherman in his place, with the removal document notarized by Hoffman himself from the USVI (Finding #2005). In October 2003, the $500,000 NYSG transfer to Schantz and $200,000 to Indyke were executed (Finding #1994). A November 2003 message to Maxwell from "Michelle" references Schantz approving vacation for Lauren on October 21, suggesting he retained some operational role into late 2003 even as his fiduciary positions were stripped (Finding #2000). The December 2004 Second Amendment completed the process by deleting his $10 million bequest (Finding #2003).

The cause of the rupture is not documented in available records. Several contextual factors merit consideration: the FTC v. Citibank litigation was active in 2002-2003, potentially creating legal exposure; the New York Post article of February 2003 publicly identified Schantz as "Epstein's lawyer" at a moment when Epstein's profile was attracting unfavorable attention (Finding #1997); and the Citibank v. Epstein parallel action in SDNY terminated in July 2003, the same window as the estate restructuring. Whether Schantz departed voluntarily, was pushed out over a dispute, or left due to concerns about the direction of Epstein's activities remains an open question. The $500,000 transfer could represent any of several things: a severance payment, the settlement of accumulated compensation, or the buyout of some other arrangement.

What is clear is that Schantz's departure triggered a fundamental reorganization of Epstein's fiduciary architecture. The replacement pattern — two trustees for one, new executors, eventual substitution of Indyke as the primary legal figure — suggests that Schantz's role had been so central that it could not be simply filled but had to be distributed. The 2012 restructuring that named Indyke, Andrew Farkas, and Jes Staley as trustees of both trusts represented a further evolution away from the original Schantz-centered model, though both trusts were ultimately revoked in October 2012 (Finding #2014).

curation.system_role: Schantz exemplifies the indispensable fiduciary layer that enabled Epstein's financial architecture: an attorney who simultaneously held trustee, executor, corporate officer, and operational management roles across multiple jurisdictions, concentrating control over legal structures, asset flows, and personnel in a single loyalist — until the relationship ruptured and required two replacements to fill his position.
open_questions: What precipitated Schantz's departure in 2003 -- was it related to the FTC v. Citibank litigation, the growing public scrutiny of Epstein, or an internal dispute? The speed and completeness of the severance suggests either a serious breach or mutual agreement to separate.

What was the nature of the $500,000 NYSG transfer in October 2003 -- severance payment, deferred compensation, buyout of the $10M bequest expectancy, or something else? The $200,000 parallel transfer to Indyke suggests a structured payout rather than ad hoc.

Is the 'Jeff Schantz' who registered as a federal lobbyist for JGW International Ltd in 2006 (LDA ID 29441) the same Jeffrey A. Schantz? If so, how did he transition from Epstein's inner circle to defense/homeland security lobbying within three years?

What role did Schantz play in the Financial Trust Company's operations beyond the Citibank/AIG matter? His sworn declarations and advisor status suggest deep involvement in FTC's investment activities, which may extend to other Epstein financial vehicles.

What is the significance of the 1996 ACRIS record (FT_1490005138449) showing Schantz as grantee on the 11 East 71st Street property? This places Schantz in the Epstein orbit at least five years before the 2001 estate plan, and the nature of the property interest (PAT document) has not been fully analyzed.
